39784-mother-goose-s-nursery-rhymes-a-co:
Mother Goose's Nursery Rhymes, a collection of alphabets, rhymes, tales, and jingles, was published at London in 1877 by George Routledge and Sons. The firm kept a New York office at 416 Broome Street. Illustrations come from Sir John Gilbert, John Tenniel, Harrison Weir, Walter Crane, and others, and some rhymes carry their music.

The contents run from A Apple Pie and A Carrion Crow sat on an Oak through the alphabet of childhood verse. Baa, baa, Black Sheep appears with its music, beside Barber, Barber, shave a Pig, Bat, Bat, come under my Hat, and Boys and Girls, come out to Play. As I was going to Saint Ives, Cross-Patch, draw the Latch, and Curly-Locks all stand in the list. The volume gathers the standard nursery stock of its century.
40641-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume 15, slice 8 of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica covers the alphabet from Kite-Flying to Kyshtym, in the dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. Transcribers explain the conventions before the articles begin: numbers following letters were printed in subscript, marks after a carat were superscript, and side-notes were moved to stand as paragraph titles. Macrons, breves, and dots below letters were not inserted.

A list of corrected misprints names the articles touched, among them Kiu-Kiang Fu, Klondike, Knaresborough, Knutsford, Korea, Kuen-Lun, and Kurdistan. The slice's own table runs from kit-fox and the naturalist John Kitto through Kizil Irmak and the Klaproths, father and son. Russian geography thickens toward the end: Kostroma as government and as town, Kotzebue the dramatist and the explorer, Kovalevsky the mathematician, Kovno, Kowtow, Kozlov, and the kraal.
46422-the-lena-pe-and-their-legends-with:
Daniel Brinton edited this study at Philadelphia in 1885 as number five in his Library of Aboriginal American Literature. Brinton was professor of ethnology and archaeology at the Academy of Natural Sciences there. His subject is the Lenâpé people and their legends, centered on a record called the Walam Olum.

The book gives the complete text and symbols of that record, in Brinton's presentation. A new translation by Brinton accompanies the carved and painted signs, he states. An inquiry into the record's authenticity closes the work, a question scholars have argued ever since Brinton put the Walam Olum before the public.
britannica-1911-aristeas-pseudonym: Aristeas is the false name past a famed Letter that tells how the Greek form of the old book came to be. He paints himself as a Greek of no Jew blood. In truth he was a Jew of a great port city in a late reign. The Letter is not true as writ, yet men of lore hold it of worth. It gives sound word on the lands of Egypt and the Jews of two past ages. Fresh forms of its Greek text came out in late years.
britannica-1911-dafydd-ab-gwilym:
Dafydd ab Gwilym, held to be the greatest of the medieval Welsh poets, who lived from about 1340 to about 1400, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bro Gynin in Cardiganshire, he was taught by a learned uncle. He became steward to his kinsman Ivor Hael of Maesaleg. He was also made tutor to the daughter of that house, and love grew between tutor and pupil.

The girl was sent to a convent in Anglesey, and the poet followed her there. On his return he kept his post and became chief bard of Glamorgan. He wrote 147 love odes to Morfudd Lawgam, whom he met in north Wales. An attempt to elope with her led to a fine he could not pay and a term in prison. Freed by friends, he went back to Maesaleg and, after the death of his patron, retired to his birthplace.
britannica-1911-homonym: Homonym is a short word entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a term used in the study of language. From a Greek word meaning having the same name, it marks words that match in sound or spelling, or both, but differ in sense. Words alike in spelling but not in sound, such as bow, are sometimes called homographs. Words alike in sound but not in spelling, such as meat and meet, are homophones.
britannica-1911-kyshtym: Kyshtym is a town of Russia, in the government of Perm, 56 miles by rail N.N.W. of Chelyabinsk. It stands on a river of the same name, which links two lakes, and in 1897 it held 12,331 people. Its official name is Verkhne-Kyshtymskiy-Zavod, or Upper Kyshtym Works. That name sets it apart from the Lower Kyshtym Works, which lie two miles farther down the same river.
doe-osti-17091588-new-uses-for-known-mol:
James Lewicki of Lawrence Livermore reports in October 2026 on turning known explosive molecules into binder plastics with energy of their own. Current bonded explosives, where crystals are held in a plastic binder, struggle to meet strength targets for next generation uses, and supply is a concern. His approach changes energetics already in use into linked polymers that grip the crystals.

A loop of computer modeling, small scale synthesis, and small scale testing screened options without long bench work. Three chemical systems emerged as strong picks for use in insensitive high explosives. Composites with firm setting binders showed clear gains in strength, and the binder itself added energy to the blast. Advanced simulations suggest strength can approach the limit set by the crystal layers.
